justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modest upward drift across horizons, starting near 327.5 for the one-day forecast, nudging to 329 at one week, and reaching 332 at one month. This gradual slope likely reflects a baseline assumption of slow positive momentum or mean-reversion tendencies in whatever underlying asset or series is being tracked, combined with any recent trend observed in the data available at the time of forecasting. The one-day estimate is essentially anchored close to the last observed value, with only minor expected movement, while the weekly and monthly estimates incorporate a small expected drift that assumes conditions remain broadly stable.

The confidence interval widths expand meaningfully as the horizon lengthens, which is a standard reflection of uncertainty compounding over time. At one day, the 90% interval spans just 15 units (320 to 335), suggesting relatively high confidence that short-term volatility will be contained. By one week, that span grows to 30 units, and by one month it widens to 58 units (303 to 361), nearly quadrupling the one-day range. This expansion accounts for the increasing probability that unexpected shocks, regime changes, or cumulative drift can push the realized value well away from the starting point. The implied daily volatility embedded in these intervals is roughly consistent with a moderate-volatility environment, neither unusually calm nor turbulent.

Several sources of uncertainty shaped these widths. At short horizons, the main risks are sudden news events, data releases, or liquidity disruptions that can cause sharp intraday moves. At longer horizons, the uncertainty broadens to include macroeconomic shifts, changes in sentiment or positioning, and the possibility that any trend assumption embedded in the point estimate simply proves wrong. Model uncertainty itself also plays a role — the forecasting approach may not fully capture tail dependencies or structural breaks.

There are meaningful risks that could push outcomes outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a sudden deterioration in macro conditions, an unexpected policy announcement, or a technical breakdown below support levels could drive the value well below 303 on a one-month horizon. On the upside, a strong positive surprise — whether fundamental, sentiment-driven, or technical — could push beyond 361. Events that are inherently unpredictable, such as geopolitical shocks or sudden liquidity crises, represent the primary tail risks that a probabilistic model based on historical patterns would systematically underestimate.
